THE biscuit family has about as many ramifications as the Forsyte family and like most families it includes members who have changed their names but who still retain their family characteristics. Thus there are regional biscuits which may be called cakes such as the Goosnargh Cakes of Lancashire, and Dorset Knobs which are nearly identical with Norfolk Hollow biscuits. The biscuit as confectionery is a comparative latecomer to the national cuisine.

brief_context: Location of a CEE meeting in 1966.
article_title: New colour coding for 3-core flexible cords
brief_extract:
International discussions
In about 1965 the CEE started discussions to form a universal colour code and eventually settled on a scheme of green/yellow for earth, and then on light blue for neutral and black for line. The United Kingdom found this quite impossible to agree to because of the use of black, and at a CEE meeting in Vienna in 1966 the United Kingdom delegation took a Government brief to say that it was willing to consider changing its colour code in order to standardise with the 19 nations of the CEE, provided that black was not the colour of the live wire. After much argument and compromise, at the end of 1966 at a further meeting of the CEE in Montreux 15 nations voted for the United Kingdom proposals that the colours should be green/yellow for earth, light blue for neutral and brown for line.

Branches
VISIT TO MARCHWOOD POWER STATION
by MRS. KINGSNORTH, Magazine Secretary, Southampton

The power station is situated on the banks of the river Test on a 148 acre site with ample cooling water facilities, good sea access if required for fuel deliveries and reasonably short connection to the National Grid System. Work started in 1952 and electricity was first generated in 1955 through its 8 turbo-alternators at 11,800 volts.

brief_context: Site of a successful conference organised by the Society.
brief_extract: A Government White Paper in 1956 focussed attention on the shortage of scientists and engineers and the need to encourage the training and employment of girls and women to fill the gap. This spurred on the Society to organise in 1957 a very successful and well publicised conference in Coventry which was attended by over 200 representatives from the educational world, industry and the Youth Employment Service. It was at this time following the death of Dame Caroline Haslett that the Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust was established to replace and extend the work of the original Trust.

brief_context: Destination for women engineers to study training and opportunities.
brief_extract: Scholarships have been awarded each year since 1957 and several of the young women who have successfully graduated are now beginning to make their mark in their chosen careers. In 1960 the Trust decided to award two special bursaries to two women engineers to enable them to visit the U.S.S.R. and to report on the training and opportunities of Russian women engineers.

brief_context: Location where Josiah Wedgwood began his pottery factory.
article_title: VISIT TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD & SONS LTD., BARLASTON
brief_extract:
BURNS, Magazine Secretary, Birmingham

Josiah Wedgwood was born in Burslem in 1730. At the age of 29 he began making the now famous Wedgwood pottery at Etruria and by 1940 the company outgrew this factory and purchased a 500-acre country estate at Barlaston where a new factory was built, employing 2,500 men and women. It was the first in the country to install electrically-fired tunnel kilns which are 273 feet long and will hold 50 kiln trucks each laden with refractory fireclay bats or platforms built in tiers on the trucks, filled with clay pieces ready for their first firing.

article_title: VISIT TO JOHN HEATHCOAT & CO., TIVERTON
brief_extract:
VISIT TO JOHN HEATHCOAT & CO., TIVERTON
by MRS A. CLAVEY, Chairman, Weston-super-Mare

This is one of the few family owned mills in the country. Until the end of the 18th century pillowlace was made on a pillow in which pins had been attached to take the yarn.

brief_context: Location of John Heathcoat's first machine lace mill.
article_title: VISIT TO JOHN HEATHCOAT & CO., TIVERTON
brief_extract: However, in 1808 the first John Heathcoat invented and patented a machine for this purpose. He opened a mill at Loughborough near to where he had been born and installed 58 machines. At that time there was great unrest in the mills, rioters smashing all the machinery.

brief_context: Country from which pure silk was imported.
article_title: VISIT TO JOHN HEATHCOAT & CO., TIVERTON
brief_extract: John Heathcoat moved to Tiverton with all his employees. Thousands of yards of pillow lace made from pure silk imported from China are despatched weekly. The thread goes through several processes before it is spun into the white gossamer-like material which eventually becomes a bridal veil.

brief_context: Region where man-made fibres from the mill are sold.
article_title: VISIT TO JOHN HEATHCOAT & CO., TIVERTON
brief_extract: Many of the old lace machines are still being used, some are 100 years old and two are 50. Of course, the interest of the mill has widened with the advance in fibres so that now man-made fibres are spun and woven for the largest manufacturers in the British Isles and overseas. It was fascinating to watch the intricate spinning of the lace, also other processes such as spinning lurex with nylon and the weaving of beautiful picot edged elastics and stretch materials for girdles.
